evidence_note: Extracted directly from the Greek of the public-domain CCAG editions. Every rule below cites a printed page that was rendered from the scan and read as an image, so the encoding does not rest on OCR. Renderings are the engine's own and are graded engine_translation_unreviewed; no modern copyrighted translation was consulted. Three recensions are kept as separate school_ids and no value is inherited across them: recension P is cod. Parisinus gr. 2425 as printed by Cumont in CCAG VIII.4; recension L is cod. Laurentianus XXVIII 34 and its nine collated witnesses as printed by Boll in CCAG I; the epitome school is the Byzantine syntagma of cod. Parisinus gr. 2506 as printed by Boudreaux in CCAG VIII.3. Editorial supplements by Cumont, Boll and Kroll are marked on the rules that depend on them. Nothing here is customer-eligible.

rules.period: early 6th century CE, Constantinople; transmitted in a 15th-century codex

conditions.trigger: a nativity is to be judged on the pinax
required_sequence: 1. prote skepsis: before all else, ease or difficulty of the birth; then the doryphoriai of the lights, whether by sect-mates or by contrary-sect planets; then whether the lights are in masculine signs or in feminine quadrants of the board; then whether the lights are well-bound or unbound to one another and to the Ascendant; then the triplicity lords of the sect light and of the Ascendant, their house rulers, the bound rulers of Sun and Moon, the dodekatemoria, and the Lots of Fortune and Daimon with their lord; then the triplicity lords of the lower midheaven
3. trite skepsis: on the angles; survives only as the tail of the argument
4. tetarte skepsis: the conjunctions and full moons, in which places they fell and what they apply to
5. pempte skepsis: the Lot of Fortune, of Daimon, of Basis, and the exaltation of the nativity, with their phases and positions
6. hekte skepsis: Anabibazon and Katabibazon, in which places and decans, and by whom beheld
7. hebdome skepsis: the dodekatemoria of the stars, above all of Sun, Moon and Ascendant
conditions.closure_condition: all seven inspections examined in this manner

conclusion.judgment: the practitioner will not err concerning the foundations of the nativity
conclusion.greek: Τούτων γὰρ πασῶν τῶν ἑπτὰ σκέψεων οὕτως ἐξεταζομένων οὐχ ἁμαρτήσῃ περὶ τὰ τῆς γενέσεως θεμέλια.
conclusion.engine_rendering: For when all these seven inspections are examined in this way, you will not go wrong about the foundations of the nativity.
conclusion.function: this is the tradition's own judgment hierarchy and the composer must execute it in this order

exceptions: The Second Inspection is entirely lost (Cumont: 'Deutera skepsis tota periit'), and the Third survives only as the end of its argument. The order may be executed only with those two slots explicitly shown as missing.
The manuscript reads ouk where Cumont prints ouch; the sense is unaffected.

conclusion.output_policy: refused absolutely. This is retained because it is the clearest demonstration that the surviving protocol judges the figure, not a client, and because it anchors a recension divergence.

'or' before 'bird' and 'some animal' are supplements from the Munich witness; Paris. gr. 2425 omits 'bird'.

conclusion.judgment: the annual year must be taken from several origins in parallel, not from the Ascendant only
conclusion.greek: μερίζων οὖν τὰ ἔτη τῆς γεννήσεως μὴ μόνον ἀπὸ τοῦ ὡροσκόπου τοὺς ἐνιαυτοὺς δέον ἐκβάλλειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπὸ Ἡλίου καὶ Σελήνης καὶ κλήρου τῆς τύχης
conclusion.engine_rendering: when distributing the years of the birth one must cast the annual periods not only from the Ascendant but also from the Sun and the Moon and the Lot of Fortune
conclusion.distinctiveness: this multi-origin requirement is one of the clearest points where the Byzantine protocol is stricter than the single-Ascendant profection commonly attributed to the Hellenistic corpus

exceptions: The chapter does not state the length of a profected step, so the pack cannot compute a profection from this passage alone.

The immediately preceding lines add ascensional times 'as the Egyptians do', the greater, mean and least years of each planet, and thirds, halves and two-thirds of those periods, plus the handings-over and receptions of the planets. Cumont marks a lacuna in that list.

rules.period: early 6th century CE, under the name of Hermes Trismegistus

scope.topic: the complete twelve-place scheme, names and significations only

conditions.order_verified_from: the volume's own index, which places the twelfth at p. 126, the first at p. 131, then 139, 144, 145, 152, 154, 158, 161, 163, 166, 170
conditions.structural_observation: all four cadent places (3, 6, 9, 12) carry the epithet metakosmios

signifies: everything accomplished before the hour of birth

place_1.stated_reason: so called because this sign rises after the rising of the Bad-Daimon and after the passage of the klimakter; here both the woman giving birth and the infant are examined

signifies: hopes from matters of the dead
place_2.note: benefics remain more idle here yet still complete the goods hoped for; it is the succedent of the Ascendant

signifies: the house in which one was born
the place of Venus, for she rejoices there
sometimes action, because it is the right trine of the midheaven
injury, especially of the fingers or bladder or feet

place_8.stated_reason: the sign is averse to the Ascendant, and so it signifies the account of death, the averse of life

place_9.note: the place of the Sun; the sign is astronomikon and metakosmion

place_10.note: the sect leaders rejoice there and give good and profitable actions

signifies: great wealth and distinguished actions when benefics are there in their own faces, houses, exaltations or bounds
action, patronage and protection at the prime of youth

exceptions: This rule encodes the NAMES and SIGNIFICATIONS only. The planet-in-place delineation tables that follow each heading are NOT encoded, because Cumont states that Rhetorius misfiled them: material belonging to the ninth place stands in the fourth and is then repeated in the ninth, and material about Mercury and the Moon printed in the fourth belongs properly to the eleventh, where it reads more correctly.

Cumont identifies two strata in the chapter: a first half agreeing closely with Valens Anthologiae II.5-14 and a second half closely tied to Firmicus Maternus III.2-7 and 13, with the two authors ordering the same material differently.

The twelfth-place entry duplicates byz.rhet.p.twelfth_place_names_and_significations, which was encoded from the collated chapter opening; the two agree and the earlier rule remains the higher-confidence record for that one place.

scope.topic: the status of the benefic/malefic classification

conditions.mercury_rule: Mercury, being shared, is good with the good and becomes malefic with the malefics
conditions.override_condition_a: malefics lying well by phase (phasis), by sect (hairesis) and by place (topos)

conclusion.core_claim: the terms benefic and malefic are said to be REPUTED (nomizontai), not absolute
conclusion.if_override_a: megalynousi tas tychas - they magnify the fortunes
conclusion.quoted_authority: Dorotheus is quoted in verse: 'the three-sided ones, though evil-working, are blunted; a star is no longer bad when it finds a good place; nor a bad place, when it welcomes a good one'
conclusion.engine_rendering: I said of the benefics and malefics that they are only RECKONED so, since often in some nativities the malefics, lying well by phase and by sect and by place, magnify the fortunes, while the benefics lying badly harm them.
conclusion.significance: this is a first-order qualification: the tradition explicitly denies that planetary benefic status is fixed

exceptions: OCR HAZARD RESOLVED: the Archive.org OCR reads 'metalynousi' here. The page image reads 'megalynousi', magnify. The rule depends on the image, not the OCR.

scope.topic: how Byzantine attributions must be handled

conditions.epitomator_claim: Houtos ho Antiochos metagenesteros estin kai Paulou tou Alexandreos kai Ouálentos - this Antiochus is later than both Paul of Alexandria and Valens
conditions.counter_evidence_1: Antiochus is cited by Porphyry and therefore lived before the third century
conditions.counter_evidence_2: the epitomator did not read Antiochus' own Thesauri; he read Rhetorius' sixth-century paraphrase of them
conditions.counter_evidence_3: in that paraphrase the opinions of Valens and Paul of Alexandria had already been inserted, which is why they surface in chapters 13-19 of the summary

conclusion.operative_rule: a Byzantine attribution is evidence about Byzantine reading, not about authorship; every rule taken from the epitome must record the epitome as its source and must not be re-attributed to the named ancient author
conclusion.engine_rendering: This Antiochus is later than both Paul of Alexandria and Valens. [The claim is false; the compiler was reading Rhetorius' paraphrase.]

exceptions: Boll's refutation is a modern editorial judgment, dated 1912, and is itself cited as such.

scope.topic: the standing of Ptolemy in the Byzantine corpus

conditions.premise_1: recapitulations of books are useful as reminders
conditions.premise_2: the Tetrabiblos needs no recapitulation at all, because a student ought to know its chapters by heart
conditions.premise_3: Ptolemy handled this laborious subject more accurately than all before him - Nechepso, Petosiris, Hermes and the like
conditions.action: the epitomator nonetheless sets out its chapter list, so as not to seem to omit the foundation

conclusion.verdict: kai tois met' auton tes technes nomos kai kanon pasin nomizetai - and by all who came after him he is reckoned the law and the canon of the art
conclusion.engine_rendering: and to all who came after him he is held to be the law and the standard of the art
conclusion.distinctiveness: explicit canonisation of one authority over the older Egyptian names is a Byzantine editorial act, and it explains why later Byzantine compendia read as Ptolemaic even when their content is Valentine or Hermetic

exceptions: Boll notes that the epitomator's chapter division differs from both the printed editions and the known manuscripts, and that Vaticanus gr. 1038 divides the proem into three chapters.

conditions.subject: the astrological booklet ascribed to Hystaspes/Odapsos, which treats Saturn in each of the twelve signs, alone and blended with the other planets, down to the parts and members of each sign, and assigns regions to signs
conditions.test_applied: whether the compiler has verified it by experience or by calculation

conclusion.verdict: homoia men oun epangellomenos estin tois allois, oupo de peira dokimasas echo e kai logismois heuron ei kai homoios tois allois peri tas hyposcheseis diamartanei
conclusion.engine_rendering: He promises much the same things as the others, but I have not yet tested it by experience, nor found by calculation whether he too, like the others, fails in his promises.
conclusion.significance: the Byzantine compiler treats the corpus as a set of claims that may fail, and names experience and calculation as the tests. This is the strongest single piece of evidence that the Byzantine layer is critical rather than merely conservative.

exceptions: The name is corrupt in the codex; Boudreaux and Cumont read 'Ho Hystaspou Odapsos'. Two other author entries in the same syntagma break off where the compiler intended to add a date and could not.
